chapter: Hite tours, postwar L.A. and the Central Avenue scene
title: The 1939 Labor Day parade and the original Jazzmobile
summary: Royal, vice president of Local 767, organized trucks with Basie, Lunceford and his band with King Cole's trio, passing Hampton's house.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Oh, he was sort of in with it. So really, what gave him the idea of that was the fact that in the year 1939, Labor Day, they had a great big parade which was always the thing in California of having the Labor Day Parade. On this particular Labor Day, two big bands were in town. It was the Count Basie Band and the Jimmie Lunceford Band. So, we had always had a walking band that represented local 767, the black local of Los Angeles. So, this time, I was vice president of the local, and I suggested to the board of directors that it would be very good if, instead of having a walking band, that we would get three trucks with the huge trailers on them, on the back of them, and invite the Basie Band and the Lunceford
Band to play each one on one truck and then we'd have one -- we'd utilize the third truck with a band from the Los Angeles local, which I was the leader of.
So, that was the original Jazzmobile that I was the founder of.

1939. We had three of these huge trucks with the trailers on them. We put pianos on each one and we had the complete Jimmie Lunceford Band and the complete Count Basie Band and my band, which my rhythm section was the King Cole Trio, with an added bass who was Red Callender. So I used two basses on it.

Johnny Miller (PHONETIC) was his bass. No, no, no, no. He had -- Wesley Prince was his bassist. Oscar Moore was the guitar player. We put this big band together and we had a battle of bands down Broadway on Labor Day, 1939, with the Lunceford Band, the Basie Band and the L.A. big band, which I was the leader of. When we finished coming back, Lionel Hampton was in town with Benny Goodman, so we pulled the truck past Lionel Hampton's house and we played a number for him. He was so enthralled about the whole thing, I think that encouraged his leaving of Benny Goodman and when he formed his

own band, he called me and tried to get the same band that he had on that truck that day that we went by, which was incorporated as King Cole was my piano player and his complete trio was part of the thing.
Who else was in your band?

Oh, let's see, well, the -- I'm trying to think who was playing in the band. I know the -- let's see, Bumps Meyers (PHONETIC) was tenor saxophone player and a boy around here was the baritone saxophone player. He passed away; I can't think of his name. Marvin Johnson was playing alto and I can't think who the other -- Andy Anderson was playing tenor and my brother was playing lead trumpet and playing all the high notes. Had another boy by the name of Jack Trainer (PHONETIC) and -- God, it's hard to remember all those things that far back. Lee Young or Oscar Moore, one of them -- Oscar Moore, I believe was my drummer, possibly Lee Young was there, too. I'm not sure. But the --

No, Oscar Bradley (PHONETIC). Oscar Moore was the guitar player. But the fantastic thing about the whole parade was the high note trumpet player. Jimmie Lunceford had Paul Webster, who was a fantastic high note player, and Duke Ellington had Al Killian, who was a fantastic high note player, and in my band, I had my brother, who was a fantastic high note player. They were just screaming all
down Broadway and it was resounding all between all the walls from the buildings. It was quite a thing.
From the making of that, I think gave Lionel Hampton an idea of what kind of band he might have liked to have had.
